newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain, Ireland won't bury N.Ireland peace.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland won't bury N.Ireland peace.

text.p: The leaders of Britain and Ireland refused to bury the Northern Ireland peace process on Saturday despite political deadlock and threats of guerrilla violence.
"We have been in a frustrating "stop" period for some time," British Prime Minister John Major said after a review of the peace process with Irish premier John Bruton.
"But I don't believe because we have been bogged down for some time that it is dead," he told reporters at a one-day informal European Union summit in Dublin.
Bruton said multi-party Belfast peace talks were the first in the province's troubled history at which all parties, pro-Irish or pro-British, were eligible to take part.
But he urged participants at the four-month-old negotitions to drop "entrenched historic positions" and compromise to steer the negotiations out of deadlock.
"It is important that all the parties in Northern Ireland should recognise that this is an historic opportunity," said Bruton.
The two leaders did not advance any new ideas to break the stalemate at the talks in a series of meetings they held while attending the EU summit, officials said.

The talks, under U.S. chairmanship, have been bogged down since day one by procedural wrangles, the absence of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, and failure to agree on how and when guerrilla groups should be disarmed.
Sinn Fein is excluded from the talks until the Irish Republican Army (IRA) declares a truce in its war against British rule, something Major said was unlikely in the near future.
"There is no sign of it (an IRA truce)," said Major.

The province's biggest political force, Ulster Unionists who want Northern Ireland to remain British, have accused the two governments of trying to ease the terms under which guerrillas should disarm to try to get Sinn Fein involved in the talks.
They insist that the terms of disarmament must be agreed at the start of the talks and have said that unless they are, the talks will go no further.
But Britain and Ireland have suggested that guerrillas should be allowed to disarm in stages and that the talks progress to build confidence in the negotiating process.
The discovery of a huge IRA arms cache in London last month has raised fears in London and Dublin of a new IRA onslaught to force Britain to soften its terms for Sinn Fein's inclusion.

At the same time officials on both sides are concerned that the IRA's foes, Protestant Loyalists who fought to keep the province British, might break their own two-year-old truce because of the IRA's failure to silence its own arms.
